title: Notice, question, predict
target: Use observations to make a prediction that can be tested.
criteria: Separate stated evidence from unsupported claims.
Extend a position pattern and state an assumption.
Name an observation that could test the prediction.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A report states that repeated observations show an object getting closer, but its future path is uncertain. Which claim is supported?
options: Its speed must be constant forever.
It will certainly collide with Earth.
Its distance is decreasing during the observed interval.
cpa.guide: Approach is stated evidence; impact, constant speed, and mass are not established.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: A table lists measured positions at 0, 2, and 4 s. A position at 6 s was calculated by extending the pattern. Which is a prediction?
options: The recorded position at 0 s only.
cpa.guide: A calculated future value is distinct from an observation.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: A rover is observed at 4, 9, and 14 m at 0, 1, and 2 s. If the same constant-velocity pattern continues, where will it be at 4 s?
cpa.guide: The pattern is +5 m each second; x(4) = 4 + 5(4) = 24 m.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A robot is at 18, 14, and 10 m at 0, 2, and 4 s. Under a constant-velocity continuation, what is its position at 6 s?
cpa.guide: Each 2 s interval changes position by −4 m; next position is 6 m.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A model predicts 24 m at 4 s. Which new observation most directly tests that prediction?
options: A measured position and uncertainty at 4 s.
A repeated statement of the prediction.
A photograph with no scale or time.
cpa.guide: A matched timed position provides a comparison with the model.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.

cpa.prompt: A constant-velocity model predicts 30 m, but a calibrated measurement is 26 ± 1 m at the same time. What should happen next?
options: Conclude that the object must have vanished.
Check the motion assumptions and inputs because the prediction lies outside the measured interval.
Ignore the measurement because models cannot be revised.
cpa.guide: The interval is 25–27 m; 30 m disagrees, but the mismatch alone does not identify the cause.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.

title: Position, distance, displacement
target: Distinguish a location, a total path length, and a change in position.
criteria: Label the origin, start, turn and finish.
Calculate path distance and signed displacement separately.
Explain why position and displacement can differ.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: On a number line with east positive, a rover starts at −3 m, turns at +5 m, and finishes at +1 m. Which label identifies its final position?
cpa.guide: Final position is the coordinate of the finish, relative to the chosen origin.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A route diagram marks a start S, a turn T, and finish F on a coordinate line. What must the origin label mean?
options: The start of every route necessarily.
cpa.guide: The chosen origin need not coincide with the start or finish.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: A robot starts at 1 m, travels to 9 m, then returns to 4 m. What are total distance and displacement?
cpa.guide: Distance = 8 + 5 = 13; displacement = 4 − 1 = +3.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A walker goes 7 m west, then 2 m east. Taking east positive, what are distance and displacement?
cpa.guide: Path length is 9; signed net change is −7 + 2 = −5.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: An object starts at −6 m and finishes at +2 m. Why are final position and displacement different?
options: Final position is +2 m relative to the origin; displacement is +8 m relative to the start.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: The coordinate origin moves 10 m east while the physical route stays unchanged. Which quantity remains unchanged?
cpa.guide: Both endpoint coordinates shift equally, so their difference is invariant.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

title: Velocity and position graphs
target: Connect a position-time graph to velocity using slope.
criteria: Read positions and elapsed times from a graph.
Find velocity from position change divided by time.
Explain the difference between speed and velocity.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A straight position-time segment runs from (2 s, 7 m) to (6 s, 19 m). What are elapsed time and position change?
cpa.guide: Use differences: 6 − 2 = 4 s; 19 − 7 = 12 m.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A position-time graph is horizontal at x = 11 m throughout the interval from 1 to 5 s. What does this show?
options: It is necessarily at the origin.
The object remains at 11 m throughout that interval.
cpa.guide: A continuously horizontal position graph shows no position change.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: Take right as positive. A cart moves steadily from 16 m to 4 m in 3 s. What is velocity?
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A robot is at −2 m at t = 1 s and +13 m at t = 6 s. What is average velocity over that interval?
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A runner travels 8 m east then 8 m west in 4 s. What are average speed and average velocity?
cpa.guide: Distance = 16 m; displacement = 0. Divide each by 4 s.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Two carts have equal average velocities over 10 s. Must their average speeds be equal?

Yes; equal displacement guarantees equal path length.
Yes; speed and velocity are identical.
No; one may travel farther while reversing direction.
cpa.guide: Equal displacement/time does not require equal distance/time.

title: Velocity graphs and components

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A velocity-time graph is constant at +3 m/s for 4 s. What is displacement?

cpa.prompt: A cart moves at −4 m/s for 2 s, then +2 m/s for 3 s. What is net displacement?

cpa.prompt: A drone’s velocity components are 7 m/s east and 2 m/s south. What is its general direction?

cpa.prompt: A velocity has components +6 m/s in x and −8 m/s in y. What is its magnitude?
cpa.guide: Magnitude = √(6² + 8²) = 10 m/s.

cpa.prompt: On a velocity-time graph, which feature represents acceleration?

cpa.prompt: A calculated interval comes from bounded measurements and a constant-velocity assumption. What does it omit unless explicitly modeled?
options: All measurement variation already included in the bounds.

cpa.prompt: A prediction gives a bounded position interval. Does that alone establish a 95% probability of being inside it?
options: No; ranges never contain any useful information.
No; a probability needs an additional statistical model.
Yes; every endpoint is equally probable automatically.
cpa.guide: Bounds constrain values under assumptions but do not specify probabilities.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

title: Vector addition
target: Add displacement vectors and use a model to explain where an object ends up.
criteria: Place arrows tip to tail without rotating them.
Combine east-west and north-south components separately.
State the resultant with units and a clear direction.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: To add displacement B to A tip-to-tail, what is done to B?
options: Rotate it until both point the same way.
Place its tip at A’s tail and reverse it.
Translate it so its tail meets A’s tip without changing its direction or length.
cpa.guide: A free vector can be translated while preserving magnitude and direction.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: After two displacements are placed tip-to-tail, where does the resultant arrow run?
options: Between the two individual arrow tips only.
From the first tail to the last tip.
From the last tip back to the first tail.
cpa.guide: The resultant connects the overall start to the overall finish.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: Displacement A is 8 m east and 3 m north. B is 5 m west and 4 m north. What are total components?
cpa.guide: Combine east-west and north-south independently: 8 − 5 = 3; 3 + 4 = 7.

criteria: Track system boundaries in an energy balance.
Distinguish thermal energy from temperature.
Use energy differences to quantify a transfer.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A block slides across a rough floor. Which system can contain the friction-related internal-energy increase in both surfaces?
options: The block with all floor interactions ignored.
Only the ruler used to measure distance.
cpa.guide: The system boundary should include the interacting surfaces when counting their internal energy.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: Mechanical energy leaves a selected system through heating. What must the energy account include?
options: An energy transfer across its boundary.
An automatic increase in kinetic energy.
A violation of total energy conservation.
cpa.guide: Energy can cross a chosen system boundary; the account must track it.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: Which distinction between temperature and internal energy is correct?
options: A warmer tiny sample must store more internal energy than any large sample.

cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: Two samples of the same material have equal mass and initial temperature. One receives twice the heating energy, with constant heat capacity and no phase change. Compare temperature rises.

Its rise is four times as large.
cpa.guide: With identical mc, ΔT = Q/(mc) scales with Q.

cpa.prompt: A constant 6 N friction force opposes a 4 m slide. What is friction’s work on the block?

title: Escape speed
target: Explain escape in an ideal gravitational-energy model.
criteria: State the zero-at-infinity energy convention.
Distinguish escape speed from circular-orbit speed.
Name neglected effects in the ideal calculation.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: With U = 0 at infinity, an object starts with U = −72 J. What minimum initial K allows it to reach infinity with zero final speed in the ideal model?
cpa.guide: Minimum escape has total E = 0, requiring K = −U = 72 J.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A probe starts with K = 95 J and U = −65 J, then coasts without losses. What is its kinetic energy at infinity?
cpa.guide: Total energy is +30 J; U approaches zero, leaving K = 30 J.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: At the same radius, how does ideal escape speed compare with circular-orbit speed?
options: Escape speed is √2 times circular speed.
Escape speed is half circular speed.
cpa.guide: v_escape = √(2GM/r); v_circular = √(GM/r).
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A spacecraft is in a stable circular orbit with no thrust. Which claim is correct?
options: It must be moving at escape speed.
It is continually falling around the planet and has not necessarily escaped.
Circular orbit means gravity is zero.
cpa.guide: Circular motion is bound by gravity; escape requires sufficient total energy.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: Which assumption belongs to the simple escape-speed model?
options: Negligible atmospheric drag and no later propulsion.
The launch speed can be zero for any planet.
Mass grows continuously as the craft rises.
Gravity becomes zero immediately above the surface.
cpa.guide: The basic energy model neglects drag and further engine work.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Interpret the stated physical model.

cpa.prompt: A launch has exactly the ideal minimum escape energy but encounters drag. What can be concluded?
options: The planet must lose all gravity.
The ideal result no longer guarantees escape because drag removes mechanical energy.
Escape is still guaranteed regardless of losses.
cpa.guide: With losses, initial energy must account for the energy removed as well.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

title: Secure wiring and finish the design
target: Document permanent connections and evaluate added mass or friction.
criteria: Check circuit continuity and mechanical security.
Preserve moving-part clearance during decoration.
Relate a design revision to an energy transfer or force.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A wire joint separates when the battery shifts. What revision addresses both mechanical and electrical reliability?
options: Secure the battery and repair the insulated joint using the supervised procedure.
Bypass the motor with a wire.
Pull the wire tighter across a gear.
Leave exposed wire touching the chassis hardware.
cpa.guide: Mechanical restraint and a secure insulated connection protect the intended circuit.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A motor stops whenever its supply wire is moved. Which testable explanation best fits?
options: Current is permanently consumed by the wire.
Moving a wire always increases battery energy.
An intermittent connection may be opening the circuit.
The motor has become a switch by definition.
cpa.guide: Motion-sensitive loss of operation suggests an intermittent path; inspect safely rather than assuming proof.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A decorative flag clears the wheel when still but bends into it during a run. Which revision should be tested?
options: Shorten or relocate the flag and check clearance during motion.
Tape it to the rotating tire.
Check only its resting position again.
cpa.guide: Dynamic clearance is needed because flexible decoration can move during operation.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Which finishing plan best preserves a working drivetrain?
options: Hide the switch beneath a permanent panel.
Glue the axle to the chassis.
Keep decorations outside gear and wheel motion and make the switch accessible.
cpa.guide: Finishing must retain mechanical clearance and control access.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

cpa.prompt: A model car’s mass changes from 0.30 kg to 0.36 kg. If net forward force remains 0.90 N, what happens to acceleration?

title: Practice runs and evidence
target: Use repeated trials to prepare an evidence-based design explanation.
criteria: Measure the actual course distance and run times.
Calculate average speed and describe variation.
Choose a final change supported by repeated evidence.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: A practice lane is measured as 3.6 m. A car takes 4.5 s from its start line to its finish line. What is average speed?
cpa.guide: Average speed = measured distance/time = 3.6/4.5 = 0.80 m/s.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: A team times motion over 2.5 m but divides the full 5 m course by that time. What must be corrected?
options: Use the distance between the actual timing start and stop points.
Double the recorded time without evidence.
Keep 5 m because larger distances give better scores.
Replace measured time with the prediction.
cpa.guide: Distance and elapsed time must describe the same interval.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: Example times over the same 4.8 m path are 6.0, 6.4, and 5.6 s. What does the spread show?
options: Performance or measurement varies, so one run is not the whole picture.
The car’s speed is exactly identical in every run.
All three readings must be discarded.
The slowest run is automatically a mistake.
cpa.guide: Repeated results reveal variation. Diagnose it rather than selecting a convenient result.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A 4.2 m run takes 7.0 s. A second run on the same path takes 6.0 s. Which comparison is correct?
options: Average speed falls from 0.70 to 0.60 m/s.
Speed doubles because time falls by 1 s.
Average speed rises from 0.60 to 0.70 m/s.
cpa.guide: 4.2/7 = 0.60 and 4.2/6 = 0.70; compare rates, not time differences alone.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: After removing a wheel rub, three example times improve from about 8 s to about 6 s over the same track. Which choice is supported?
options: Undo it because lower time means lower speed.
Declare a guaranteed win on every surface.
Keep the adjustment provisionally and confirm it with the same controlled test.
Credit a different change that was not made.
cpa.guide: Repeated faster times support the tested adjustment, within the tested conditions.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

One run proves all future results.
cpa.guide: Multiple simultaneous changes confound causal attribution. Isolate one factor and repeat.

title: Race, explain and transfer
target: Evaluate a model against measured performance and defend design decisions.
criteria: Report measured distance, time and average speed.
Compare actual speed with a stated prediction.
Use evidence to explain three physical design choices.

authoring.limitations: Reasoning evidence only. Multiple choice does not certify physical performance. Teacher reviews before assigning and rates mastery separately.

cpa.prompt: In a supplied race example, a car travels 6.3 m in 9.0 s. Which report has the correct average speed and units?
cpa.guide: 6.3/9.0 = 0.70 m/s. Average speed uses length per time, not acceleration units.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Which report separates a real observation from a model prediction?
options: “Our car must match the example because it is the same color.”
“Measured 0.60 m/s,” copied from the model without timing.
“Predicted and measured mean the same thing.”
“Measured time: 8.2 s over 4.1 m; model speed: 0.60 m/s.”
cpa.guide: Measured distance and time are evidence; a predicted speed comes from a model and must be labeled separately.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.

cpa.prompt: A model predicts 0.80 m/s. Example measured average speed is 0.60 m/s. Relative to the prediction, how much lower is the measured speed?
cpa.guide: Difference = 0.20; 0.20/0.80 × 100 = 25%. Use the stated reference in the denominator.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Apply the physical relationship to new data.

cpa.prompt: Measured speed is below a no-slip, no-loss prediction. Which explanation is appropriately cautious?
options: Rubbing, slip, or lower loaded motor rate could contribute; test these possibilities.
The measurement proves energy was destroyed.
Only the wheel color can explain it.
The model must be exact because it contains numbers.
cpa.guide: Ideal assumptions can omit losses and load effects. A mismatch does not uniquely identify its cause.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Select a claim supported by the stated evidence and assumptions.

cpa.prompt: Which explanation connects three design choices to physics?
options: Larger wheels always win; alignment never matters; current disappears at the motor.
Larger wheels change distance per turn; alignment limits unequal rubbing; secure wiring maintains the intended circuit.
Wheel size, alignment, and wiring only change appearance.
Paint creates power; alignment stores charge; wires provide fuel.
cpa.guide: The correct set connects geometry, forces, and electrical continuity without unconditional performance claims.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.

demand.evidence: Compare evidence and identify a physical relationship.

cpa.prompt: A new race course starts on a steeper ramp. Why might a slower gear reduction be useful even though its ideal top speed is lower?
options: It guarantees greater speed and torque at unchanged power.
It can provide greater axle torque to overcome the required driving load.
It creates energy from the gears.
It removes gravity from the car.
cpa.guide: A reduction trades rotational speed for torque. Whether it improves the race requires testing the new course.
cpa.freshness: New scenario and/or model data, independently answerable without worksheet answers.
